Free tools

Claude Code Settings Check

Paste a settings.json (and, optionally, settings.local.json) and get every structural mistake in its hooks and permissions sections flagged in seconds — a matcher that can't compile, a hook with no command, a rule with unbalanced parentheses, a rule duplicated across lists, and a rule that contradicts itself across the two files.

Structural checks, not a runtime test. This tool never runs your hooks and never calls an LLM — it only looks at the text you paste and flags known failure shapes in it. It does not know which file or list Claude Code honours when two rules disagree; it only tells you that they disagree.

1. Paste your settings.json

The project's shared, committed configuration. Nothing here is uploaded — everything runs in this page.

Findings

Paste a settings.json above, or load the example, then press Check.

    Usage is optional, stays in this browser, and counts only that a check ran or a summary was copied. Nothing you paste — no settings, hook commands, or file paths — is ever recorded, uploaded, or sent to an analytics service. Uncheck to turn it off. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control disable counting automatically.

    Common questions

    What does this tool check in a settings.json file?

    Two sections: hooks (a matcher regex that fails to compile, a matcher group with no hook commands, a hook entry with an empty or missing command, and event/type names checked against this tool's documented list as a caution) and permissions (a rule string with unbalanced parentheses, trailing text after the closing parenthesis, an empty specifier, leading or trailing whitespace, a rule duplicated within one list, and a rule appearing in more than one of allow/deny/ask).

    Does this tool contact a network or Anthropic's servers?

    No. Every check is a deterministic, structural check against the text you paste, entirely in your browser. It never uploads anything and never calls an LLM.

    Does a clean result mean my hooks and permissions work correctly?

    No. This tool checks the shape of the file, not Claude Code's runtime behaviour. A hook can be perfectly well-formed and still not do what you intended, and this tool has no way to observe that. It also does not know which file or list Claude Code honours when two rules disagree -- it only tells you that they disagree, and points you at the current documentation to resolve it.

    Why check settings.local.json against settings.json together?

    Because a rule that contradicts itself across the two files is invisible if you only ever look at one of them -- a deny in the shared, committed settings.json and an allow for the exact same rule in your own settings.local.json is easy to introduce and easy to miss, since nothing about either file alone looks wrong.

    No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not a guarantee of how Claude Code will behave at runtime, and it does not replace testing your configuration in the agent you actually run it in. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for checking any finding against Claude Code's current documentation. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

    Privacy. Everything runs client-side in your browser. The settings text you paste, and every finding this tool produces, never leaves your device — there is no upload, no server-side processing, and no third-party analytics vendor.

    Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record.

    Auditing an MCP server's launch config instead? See MCP Config Risk Check. Checking a Claude Code Skill's frontmatter instead? See Skill Manifest Check. Checking a pasted file for hidden or invisible Unicode instead? See Hidden Unicode Check. Checking a Claude Code subagent definition instead? See Claude Code Subagent Check. Checking a hook's command text for dangerous shapes instead of the file's structure? See Claude Code Hooks Security Check.

vs-reading-the-settings-json-by-eye.html.text:
← Claude Code Settings Check

Claude Code Settings Check vs. reading the settings.json by eye

Reading a short settings.json with one obviously empty hook command catches that command. It reliably misses a matcher regex that looks fine but fails to compile, a permission rule with one stray parenthesis, a rule duplicated across allow/deny/ask, and a rule that quietly contradicts itself between settings.json and settings.local.json — which is what this free, no-upload checker computes exactly, in one pass.

Where reading it yourself stops being enough

Anyone editing a settings.json already does this: read the hooks and permissions blocks and decide whether they look right before trusting them to fire unattended. For a single hook with an obviously empty command, that read catches it. The problem is the other checks below are not the kind of thing a skim of rendered JSON reliably surfaces, especially once a project carries a committed settings.json and a personal settings.local.json side by side.

What you're trying to confirmReading the settings.json yourselfThis checker
A hook entry has an empty or missing command.Works. This is the one case a plain read reliably catches.Also catches it, in the same pass as everything below.
A hook matcher regex compiles at all, rather than just looking like plausible syntax.A string like Bash( reads as ordinary regex text; nothing about it looks wrong until something tries to compile it.Actually compiled, the same way every time, against every matcher in the file.
A hook event or type name matches this tool's documented list, as a caution against a typo.Requires recognizing nine event names and one hook type from memory while reading.Checked against a dated reference list automatically.
A permission rule string has balanced parentheses, a single non-empty specifier, and no stray whitespace.A rule with one extra or missing parenthesis reads as roughly right at a glance.Parsed and checked against the exact grammar, every rule.
A rule appears more than once within one list, or in more than one of allow/deny/ask.Easy with three or four rules; easy to miss once a file accumulates dozens across a project's history.Every rule compared against every other rule in both files, exactly.
A rule in settings.json contradicts one for the same specifier in settings.local.json.Each file reads as correct in isolation; most editors don't show both side by side.Both files' full rule lists compared against each other, rule by rule.
Re-checking an entire settings.json (and its local override) again after adding or editing one hook or rule.One hook or rule at a time, remembered by hand, every time something changes.One paste, both files, every time.

A quick read is still the fastest way to catch an obviously empty command in a short file, and this checker is not doing anything a careful line-by-line audit couldn't — it is reading the same hooks and permissions blocks a careful audit would, just compiling every matcher and comparing every rule automatically instead of leaving the comparison to be remembered by hand.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: the browser page parses JSON you paste entirely in your own browser. It never sends your settings anywhere.

Common questions

Can't I just read my settings.json myself?

For a short file with one hook and an obviously empty command, yes -- that case is visible on a single read. What reading does not reliably catch is a matcher regex that looks like valid syntax but fails to compile, a permission rule with one extra or missing parenthesis, a rule duplicated across allow/deny/ask, or a rule that contradicts itself between settings.json and settings.local.json. Those need every rule and every matcher checked the same mechanical way, not remembered while skimming a file with a dozen hooks and rules in it.

Why is a regex that fails to compile easy to miss on a read-through?

Because a matcher string like Bash( or [unclosed reads as plausible regex syntax at a glance -- nothing about the shape looks obviously wrong until something actually tries to compile it. A hook behind a broken matcher never fires and produces no error, no log line, and nothing to notice; the only way to know is to run the same compile step this tool runs, against every matcher in the file, not skim the string and judge it by eye.

Why is a cross-file contradiction between settings.json and settings.local.json easy to miss?

Because each file reads as correct in isolation -- a deny in the shared, committed settings.json and an allow for the exact same rule string in your own settings.local.json are two ordinary-looking lines in two files most editors don't show side by side. Catching the contradiction means holding both files' full rule lists in mind at once and comparing them rule by rule, which is a pairwise check a tool runs the same way every time and a person reviewing one file at a time does not.

What about a rule duplicated across allow, deny, and ask?

A rule string repeated in two of the three lists, or twice within one list, does not look wrong on its own -- each occurrence is a valid rule. Noticing the repeat means comparing every entry in allow against every entry in deny and ask, which is easy with three or four rules and easy to miss once a settings.json accumulates dozens across a project's history.

Is this page making a live comparison against a tool or company?

No. This page describes a manual habit anyone editing a Claude Code settings.json already has -- reading the hooks and permissions sections by eye before trusting them. It names no competing product or company. The checker itself makes no network request of any kind: the browser page parses pasted JSON in your own browser, and nothing you paste is ever uploaded.

You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for checking any finding against Claude Code's current documentation. Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record.
